items.title: AI chip smugglers exploit trade control loophole to bring banned HBM from South Korea into China — expensive memory chips packaged with cheap, unsanctioned processors to become legal exports - Tom's Hardware
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
A memory smuggler has detailed how he gets export-controlled HBM chips from South Korea into China using a loophole. According to The Information , the smuggler owns a chip design firm that build cheap, low-performing processors that fall under the U.S. and South Korea's export controls. They are then paired with expensive HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, that, on their own, are banned for export to China. But because export control rules only look at the performance of the server processor and not at the other components attached to it, this allows the HBM chips attached inside them to slip under the radar and make their way into China.
Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs
While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market
The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push
China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab
China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained
It's not a risk-free operation, though. Once the mediocre processors with high-end memory chips land in Hong Kong and are smuggled across the border into Shenzhen in the luggage of commuters that cross between the two regions daily, they end up in workshops where technicians heat up the boards to soften the solder, gingerly lift the crucial memory chips, and discard the rest of the components. Despite having a high failure rate, the high price of HBM chips makes the procedure quite lucrative.
A Shenzhen-based chip broker has been making big money matching up suppliers such as the smuggler and companies that are desperate for HBM. "A year ago, a single HBM3E unit changed hands in China for several hundred dollars," he tells the publication. "Today it's about $4,000." With an AI chip requiring six to eight high-end memory chips, that means the broker is raking in $24,000 to $32,000 for every AI GPU.
Chinese AI labs face this exact memory chip bottleneck when acquiring AI GPUs. While Chinese memory manufacturer CXMT has already begun risk production of HBM3E and is expected to mass produce them by the end of this year , it's still reportedly suffering from low yield, which makes their chips expensive to produce and procure. We see this with Huawei's Ascend 950DT, its current top-of-the-line processor that goes for about $37,000 — it offers similar pricing to Nvidia's B200 AI GPU but only delivers half the performance of the previous-generation H100.
Huawei has reportedly said that its next-generation flagship AI processor, the 960DT, would deliver a similar performance as the H100. However, since the company cannot purchase HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, and Chinese memory manufacturers do not have the capacity to supply all its chip demands, Huawei told customers that they have to find the HBM that these servers need themselves. This would further fuel the demand for these chips, increase the price and make it more lucrative for smugglers to set up similar operations.
But given that this method of moving HBM chips into China is becoming more popular, the smuggler fears that South Korean and U.S. authorities would clamp down on their operations soon. Washington has been going down hard on activities like this, and we've seen high-profile arrests including some Super Micro executives and the CEO of a California-based tech company . Other countries like Taiwan and Malaysia have been ramping up their anti-smuggling activities, too, so it's probably just a matter of time before Seoul follows suit.

items.content:
Emergency responders comb through rubble after deadly strike on Ukrainian aid centre – video
Russia bombs humanitarian hub in Ukraine, killing at least 31 people
Other overnight strikes targeted power plants across Ukraine, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people
Russia has bombed a humanitarian hub in southern Ukraine , killing at least 31 people and leaving dozens missing, as part of a wave of strikes across the country.
Other overnight Russian strikes targeted power plants across Ukraine, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people, as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned that the US was distracted by its midterm elections.
In total, Russia had launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, Zelenskyy said in an online post.
“The Russians think America won’t notice this signal of theirs,” he said. “But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes,” he said.
The barrage came just a day after a rare local ceasefire in neighbouring Kherson ended, underscoring the limits of the temporary truce.
The deadliest guided-bomb attack first targeted a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a village in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region, and then took aim at a nearby shelter.
Rescuers carry the body of a person killed by a Russian airstrike inside an underground shelter of a local school, which was used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia region. Photograph: Reuters The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the regional military administration, said on Tuesday. At least five people were hurt. Semikin said 48 people were considered missing.
As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used torches to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials.
Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app
Efforts to rescue people on Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages from the site.
Ukrainian soldiers stand among the rubble after a Russian airstrike on the humanitarian aid hub. Photograph: Reuters The attack, he said, had shown that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the past week’s ceasefire in the embattled southern city of Oleshky , brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump.
“Russians continue to demonstrate, time and again, their hatred of Ukraine and everything that exists here,” Zelenskyy said.
In the north-east region of Kharkiv, a combined Russian missile and drone attack had wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said. A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients had been transferred to other medical facilities, said the head of the regional military administration, Oleh Syniehubov.
“If Russia genuinely ‌wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps. We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people,” Zelenskyy said.
The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied Oleshky. It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned “at the moment”.
US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine were due to resume next week, the US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.
Donald Trump, who pledged during his election campaign to end the war in a single day, has repeatedly pushed for a settlement but has so far failed to secure a breakthrough.
The latest round of talks is scheduled for 10-11 November in Abu Dhabi, according to Witkoff, amid growing concerns in Kyiv and among its European allies over Trump’s increasingly close ties with Moscow and discussions of potential business deals between the US and Russia.
Trump rewards Putin and betrays Ukraine with Russia diesel deal - The Latest
Russia announced on Tuesday that its delegation would be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline former culture minister who has headed several previous rounds of negotiations with Ukraine.
Medinsky’s earlier appointment as chief negotiator was met with scepticism by Ukrainian officials and analysts, who questioned whether he had the authority to make meaningful concessions. A key architect of the historical revisionism used by Putin to justify his invasion of Ukraine, Medinsky has long promoted the Kremlin’s narrative that Ukraine is inseparable from Russia.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, arrived in Berlin for talks with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Germany has become Ukraine’s largest provider of military aid since Merz took office in May 2025, overtaking the US as American support has declined.
The Ukrainian president is also expected to attend this year’s Berlin Security Conference.
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.
“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets , so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”.
Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

items.title: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific - Al Jazeera
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific on social media
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.
Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.

list 2 of 3 How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge
list 3 of 3 How would Tehran respond if the US and Israel bomb Iran again?
“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”
Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .
The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the US and the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it.
Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. The Asia Pacific was again hit harder than most. Some 15 countries were hit with tariffs, with Cambodia facing a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Still, some analysts see a narrow opening on tariffs.
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect Congress to act is on China.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China’s access to technology, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

Iran says 3 oil tankers hit naval mines, catch fire in Strait of Hormuz
IRGC Navy says vessels had switched off navigation and identification systems while using unauthorized routes through strategic waterway
İSTANBUL Three oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while navigating “unauthorized” routes through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Tuesday.
The Tasnim News Agency, citing a statement from the IRGC Navy’s public relations office, said the three tankers experienced explosions and severe fires after entering “unauthorized” shipping routes with their navigation and identification systems switched off.
The incidents occurred in the early hours of Tuesday, with the resulting fires illuminating the eastern section of the strait throughout the night, according to the statement.
The IRGC said the tankers had been abandoned near the southern shores of the Strait of Hormuz and remained engulfed in flames.
It said Iranian regulations governing navigation through the strait have repeatedly been communicated to vessels through radio broadcasts and official naval notices.
The IRGC warned that ships disregarding these regulations and cooperating with the US military to cross unauthorized routes could face similar incidents.
The statement also rejected claims by the commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM) about conditions in the strait, accusing him of using archival footage on social media to misrepresent the situation.
The IRGC did not identify the tankers or provide details about their crews, casualties, or the extent of the damage.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the reported incidents.
The Strait of Hormuz has become a major flashpoint since the US and Israel launched their military offensive against Iran on Feb. 28.
Iranian forces have tightened control over maritime traffic through the strategic waterway, while Tehran has accused Washington of maintaining a naval blockade.
The latest statement follows a separate announcement by Iran’s Navy on Monday that an oil tanker had struck a naval mine and caught fire in an area described as prohibited and unsafe east of the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
items.summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.
items.content:
Image caption, A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise less than 50km (31 miles) from the Russian border in Finland
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.
But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."
Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force â Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.
He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".
Image caption, Ukrainian troops take part in urban warfare training at a military base in England in 2023
Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.
Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.
Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.
Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.
As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.
However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.
In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.
Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.
It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.
Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.
Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

Share US hits Qeshm Island, Pezeshkian signals more diplomacy: Iran war latest on social media
Fishing boats sit idle in the Strait of Hormuz, near Qeshm Island, Iran [File: Majid Saeedi/Getty Images]
Amid growing concerns about renewed attacks on Iran following Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, US forces have struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what officials have reportedly described as a defensive measure.
In the first attack since June on Qeshm Island, which serves as the primary platform for Iran’s “asymmetric” naval power , according to analysts, the US strikes come as both sides continue to adopt military and diplomatic postures.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 How will the Iran war shape the outcome of the US midterm vote?
list 2 of 3 How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge
list 3 of 3 China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetings
Mediation efforts led by Qatar are continuing in a bid to avert a return to all-out war, which began on February 28 when the US and Israel launched strikes across Iran, triggering the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz, surging oil and gas prices and massive damage to military, civil and energy facilities around the Gulf.
Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island late on Monday, as US media reported that the US military had carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.
The blasts came in rapid succession, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying over the island, located off Iran’s southern coast along the waterway.
According to The Wall Street Journal, which quoted an unnamed official, the strikes on Monday night appeared limited and were not a resumption of a major operation.
The Associated Press news agency also quoted an unnamed US official as saying Washington had conducted the defensive strikes against “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”.
The attack came after IRNA reported that the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had destroyed a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US first struck a critical desalination plant on Qeshm Island on March 7 – one week into the war. The strike, which Tehran branded a “flagrant crime” against civilians, cut off freshwater supplies to 30 surrounding villages.
A satellite view of Qeshm Island, Hormozgan Province, Iran, within the Strait of Hormuz region on January 17, 2026 [Gallo Images/Orbital Horizon/Copernicus Sentinel Data 2026] But isn’t diplomacy ongoing?
It is, but it is fragile, and mixed messages are coming from both sides.
Qatari mediators have been engaged in indirect talks with Iranian officials in recent days. They have passed messages between the two sides, but the talks appeared to come to an end on Monday with no news of a breakthrough.
An official briefed on the talks told the Reuters news agency that Iran’s delegation had departed from Doha on Sunday, but that a draft proposal was still being circulated, without elaborating on the content.
Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi regarding a version of a draft US-Iran deal which has been under negotiation for the past eight days, an official told Reuters.
Araghchi told IRNA on Monday: “Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals, and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington.”
Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also told a news conference on Monday that the “ball” was in the US’s court as Iran’s demands were “clear and logical”.
He said the plan Iran submitted in September to end the war remained the focus of talks, but that the proposal could be shortened and implemented in “two days”, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to talks about Iran’s nuclear programme.
On Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had given the government “certain authorities” over talks with the US, local media reported.
The president added that Tehran would look to resolve the conflict through dialogue.
Khamenei’s apparent approval of diplomacy marks a change since the breakdown of the June memorandum of understanding , which allowed a brief ceasefire and peace negotiations, when the supreme leader said the US could not be trusted.
For the US side, Vice President JD Vance also told reporters on Monday that he was hopeful for a diplomatic solution – just hours before the strikes on Qeshm Island.
“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance said. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reiterated on Tuesday that Iran’s response to any US “miscalculation”, such as launching strikes, would be unpredictable.
“The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit,” he said.
Oil prices dropped by more than 7 percent on Monday. In response, Trump wrote on his Truth Social account that people believe the war with Iran will not resume as mediation efforts continue.
“Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!” Trump wrote.
He told media at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC, that it looked like efforts were “coming together very nicely”.
“That’s why I guess the oil prices dropped. People found out about it.”
However, Trump also told the US media outlet Axios before his post on Truth Social that he was “in no rush” to decide whether to resume strikes on Iran.
“One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline, and their people are getting very tired of it,” Trump told Axios in an interview.
The US midterm elections  are being viewed as the inflexion point for Trump’s decision on what path he takes next.
The president has suggested several times that he could attack Iran following the vote and told the Right Side Broadcasting Network (RSBN) on Sunday that the conflict would end “very soon one way or the other”, adding that Tehran would either “make a deal, or we’ll just end it”.
Observers say the US will likely renew strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities if they do resume.
In particular, this could include Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain , a highly fortified site that contains two tunnel complexes buried deep underground, and which Trump told US outlet Newsmax last month could be a target. He said the US “may have to go there. We’ll take a shot at that one. We’ll knock it out fast.”

items.content:
Ross 308 chickens at a farm in France in 2024. The breed, labelled the turbo chicken, is the most widespread in Danish poultry production. Photograph: Damien Meyer/AFP/Getty Images
Ross 308 chickens at a farm in France in 2024. The breed, labelled the turbo chicken, is the most widespread in Danish poultry production. Photograph: Damien Meyer/AFP/Getty Images
Denmark pushes for EU ban on ‘turbo chickens’ as secret footage causes outrage
Minister says government will work towards banning fast-growing breed across country and throughout EU
The Danish government is pursuing a national ban on “turbo chickens” and is calling for the fast-growing breed to be prohibited across Europe .
The move comes amid widespread outrage over allegations of lawbreaking by one of Denmark’s big chicken producers.
According to a TV2 documentary broadcast last week, producer Christian Tvergaard broke Danish law by giving chickens only half the amount of darkness a day that is required, in order to encourage them to eat more. The documentary featured secretly filmed footage from a chicken coop in North Jutland.
The Ross 308 breed, labelled the turbo chicken, is the most widespread in Danish poultry production. It grows from about 50 grams to 2kg in just 33 days. Such rapid growth can lead to problems with the animal’s bones and organs. Other chicken breeds take between 46 and 63 days to reach the same weight.
Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare, Christian Rabjerg Madsen, said he discouraged Danes from buying turbo chickens, telling the broadcaster: “I want to work for a national ban. But it’s clear that this is something that needs to be investigated both legally and economically.” He added: “Now we will work for a national ban, we will work for a ban at EU level.”
Christian Rabjerg Madsen. Photograph: Sebastian Elias Uth/Reuters In response to the documentary, Tvergaard has admitted to making some wrong decisions. He told TV2: “I look inward and must admit that I have made some wrong decisions. There is no excuse for that, but I can learn from it and correct where I have not done well enough.
“And I have done that, both when it comes to the lighting programme and a number of the workflows we have in the stable, where both procedures and the roster have been tightened up.”
The proposal for the ban on turbo chickens is gaining political momentum and attracting cross-party support in Denmark. But industry figures warn that to be effective, any ban must include imported chickens as well.
Klement Hinkbøl Ribergaard, the chief executive of chicken producer Danpo, said: “If Denmark alone bans the production of fast-growing chickens while shops, restaurants and consumers in the Danish market can continue to buy imported, fast-growing chicken of more or less questionable quality, we risk a situation in which animal welfare certainly does not benefit.”
With fast-growing breeds so prominent across the EU, it would mark a landmark shift. According to Eurogroup for Animals , 95% of chickens in the bloc are now raised in intensive systems and bred to produce the cheapest amount of meat possible, creating a “race to the bottom”.
“Fast-growing breeds are inherently predisposed to suffering, with their bodies growing so quickly they can barely stand on their legs,” said Reineke Hameleers, the advocacy group’s chief executive. “Denmark’s political willingness to stop this is an example that should be followed by the EU, for it presents the progressiveness this industry needs, one that is backed up by scientific evidence.”
Britta Riis, chief executive of Animal Protection Denmark, said turbo chickens were the result of a “deeply unethical and grotesque form of breeding” that led to “systematic abuse” and considerable suffering for the birds. The organisation is calling for all chickens to be bred for the same amount of time as organic breeds, which is 56 days.
Animal welfare has featured heavily in public debate in recent months in Denmark. The issue of pig farming dominated the last general election to such an extent that it was nicknamed the “pig election” .
The country is due to stop mink farming by August 2029 after the current government decided not to seek an EU exemption on the practice.

items.title: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in nine countries
items.summary: Supermarkets have reported problems from Estonia and Sweden to Portugal and Italy and many retainers have been forced to discard food.
items.content:
Image caption, Investigations have begun in several European countries in response to the cyber-attacks
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least nine European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
Image caption, Supermarket chains said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared as high as 50C
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy , Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland , 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
In Portugal , the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven IntermarchÃ© stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland , irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia , at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
Image caption, Food losses are estimated in the tens of millions of euros
In the UK , the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

items.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
items.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.
items.content:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.
Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.
Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

items.title: AI Bubble Fears Grow as Morgan Stanley Warns of Another Chip Selloff; Equal-Weight ETF Offers Shelter from Concentration - BigGo Finance
items.summary: AI Bubble Fears Grow as Morgan Stanley Warns of Another Chip Selloff; Equal-Weight ETF Offers Shelter from Concentration  BigGo Finance
items.content:
AI Bubble Fears Grow as Morgan Stanley Warns of Another Chip Selloff; Equal-Weight ETF Offers Shelter from Concentration
Morgan Stanley strategist Mike Wilson expects semiconductor shares to fall another 10% to 15% before bottoming around mid-November, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index possibly reaching 9,500. The iShares Semiconductor ETF has already dropped 28.1% from its June peak. Analysts point to concentration rather than valuation as the core vulnerability: Nvidia makes up about 21% of the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the top 10 holdings 69% of assets, while the top 10 names represent 47% of QQQ and 39% of SPY. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF cuts the Magnificent Seven's combined weight to about 1.37% and technology to roughly 16%, offering less upside in exchange for reduced concentration risk.
Morgan Stanley Nvidia Corp Mike Wilson Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF VanEck Semiconductor ETF iShares Semiconductor ETF Philadelphia Semiconductor Index Amazon.com Inc Alphabet Inc Microsoft Corp Tal Schwartz AI Funds Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF Invesco QQQ Trust SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
Morgan Stanley's chief U.S. equity strategist, Mike Wilson, expects chip stocks to shed another 10% to 15% before finding a floor around mid-November, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index potentially sliding to 9,500 points. The call lands as investors grapple with a market where a handful of artificial intelligence winners dominate index weights and where the gap between AI infrastructure spending and measurable returns keeps widening.
The warning is not a forecast of collapse so much as a recognition of how narrow the market's foundation has become. Wilson ties the pressure to tightening financial conditions and to a structural dependency: chipmaker revenue rests on the capital commitments of a very small group of large technology companies. Should those buyers trim hardware orders to protect their own cash flow, several suppliers would be hit at the same time.
That dynamic is already visible in the tape. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) has fallen 28.1% from its June peak of $656 to $471.51, sliding more than 8% in a single session after Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to a range of $15 billion to $16 billion, well below expectations. Intel shares lost 29% of their value in the aftermath. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed 20% below its June record in July and dropped 6.7% on Oct. 22 alone, according to Benzinga.
The cash-flow math behind the anxiety is stark. Amazon reported negative trailing 12-month free cash flow of $42.4 billion, while Alphabet posted roughly $9 billion in negative quarterly free cash flow, figures cited in the same report. Morgan Stanley projects hyperscaler AI spending will reach $1.58 trillion by 2027.
Concentration, not valuation, is the real fault line
Tal Schwartz, founder of Ai Funds, whose AI Bubble Pop Index scores overall bubble risk at just 3 out of 20 based on Oct. 2 readings, argues the headline number offers false comfort. "It doesn't score sectors, so a low reading isn't a clean bill of health for any of them," he told Benzinga.
Asked which major AI-linked fund is most exposed to a spending slowdown, Schwartz pointed to the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH). Nvidia Corp (NVDA) accounts for roughly 21% of its portfolio and the top 10 holdings make up 69% of assets, according to Morningstar data. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) holds about 90 names, with its top 10 at roughly 33% and Nvidia below 3%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF carries Nvidia at approximately 8%.
"The more a fund depends on one group of customers' spending, the more a capex slowdown could hurt it," Schwartz said.
He models a hypothetical 20% cut in hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending over the next 12 months as a direct hit to chip equipment makers, memory producers, accelerator and networking suppliers, and the optical and power names common in thematic funds. High fixed costs mean a revenue dip hits earnings harder, and valuations already assume years of growth. In the 2022 chip downturn, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 45% from its January high to its October low. The twist, Schwartz noted, is that the hyperscalers themselves could hold up better, since spending less lifts their free cash flow.
Even broad index funds carry the exposure. At the end of September, the top 10 holdings represented about 47% of the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and 39% of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY). "The risk runs deeper than the weights," Schwartz said, because Nvidia sells to Microsoft Corp (MSFT), Amazon.com Inc (AMZN), Alphabet Inc (GOOGL) and Meta Platforms Inc (META), all of which sit in the same funds. "A cap-weighted index is static by design. It owns the most of whatever has already risen the most, and it rides every decline."
The Magnificent Seven -- Apple (AAPL), Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Tesla (TSLA) -- account for roughly one-third of the S&P 500's total market capitalization. A passive investor in a cap-weighted S&P 500 fund therefore has more than 30 cents of every dollar in seven stocks, most trading at elevated valuations. The cap-weighted index's Shiller CAPE ratio stands at 40.7, near its second-highest reading in 155 years.
The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) holds the same 500 companies but assigns each roughly 0.2% of assets, cutting the Magnificent Seven's combined weight to about 1.37%. Technology accounts for approximately 16% of the fund versus roughly 40% in SPY. The structure dilutes the extreme multiples of the largest names across 500 positions, producing a materially lower valuation than the cap-weighted benchmark, and it charges a 0.20% expense ratio.
The cost is performance in a momentum-driven market. Over most 10-year stretches that included a sustained mega-cap technology bull run, equal weighting trailed the cap-weighted S&P 500, and investors convinced the AI trade has further to go would capture less upside. Schwartz also cautioned that equal weighting shifts exposure toward banks, cyclicals and rate-sensitive stocks.
iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) ~8% Five names ~39%
Global X AI & Technology ETF (AIQ) <3% ~33%
Note: Figures reflect Morningstar data and end-September holdings as cited in the report; SOXX concentration refers to Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and Intel.
Three of the ten indicators in the AI Bubble Pop Index currently flash yellow: AI-linked layoffs, cheaper Chinese AI models and the yield curve. Big Tech capital expenditure already consumes about 80% of operating cash flow, with spending above 100% triggering a warning. Schwartz sees Chinese "AI dumping" as the likeliest path to disappointment, because it would land on a highly concentrated system.
He draws a parallel to Cisco Systems Inc (CSCO) during the dot-com era. "Cisco sold the routers that built the internet, Nvidia sells the chips that power AI, and both became the world's most valuable company," Schwartz said. Cisco fell 38% in early 1997 on slowing sales and 37% in 1998 during the Russia and LTCM crisis, yet gained about 590% in the two years before its March 2000 peak. Nvidia lost $589 billion in market value in a single day on the DeepSeek scare in January 2025 and recovered nearly all of it within weeks.
"Scares like these are swings. Cisco fell 89% by October 2002 only after its customers stopped buying," he said, adding that what ends a boom has not changed: customers reducing spending.
The implication for investors is that the debate has moved from whether AI is real to whether the companies funding it can demonstrate returns before their own balance sheets force a pause. Wilson's view that the correction has been grinding on for months fits that framing. For those unwilling to abandon U.S. equities but uneasy about a market where a single capex decision can hit both supplier and customer in the same portfolio, the choice comes down to accepting lower upside in exchange for less concentrated downside.

Oil prices climb after U.S. strikes Iran's Qeshm Island
Brent crude was up 0.97% on Tuesday at $105.77 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate was up 0.97% to $97.41.
The rebound in oil prices come a day after the U.S. and Iranian presidents signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to Iran war.
Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
This photo shows fuel tanks at the fuel depot near LaGuardia airport in the Queens borough of New York City on Oct. 5, 2026.
Oil prices climbed on Tuesday after the U.S. reportedly struck Iran's Qeshm Island late Monday, one day before the midterm elections.
Brent crude was up 1.75% on Tuesday at $106.60 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate was up 1.7% to $98.10.
Oil prices rebounded a day after the U.S. and Iranian presidents signaled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the Iran war, which saw oil prices sell off over 7% on Monday.
But before this development, Brent prices were at their highest since 2022, as fears of further U.S. strikes on Iran after the midterms mounted.
Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
But despite these strikes, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.

items.title: Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station
items.summary: Europe is scrambling to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs.
items.content:
Brookfield plans $27 billion AI data center at power station; Drax rises 8%
Brookfield is planning a data center with more than one gigawatt of capacity at a site in England.
The asset manager estimated that the potential investment for the project could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion).
Drax Group, which operates the power station the facility will be housed at, saw shares rise more than 8% on Tuesday morning.
Brookfield is targeting a massive artificial intelligence data center in the north of England, as Europe scrambles to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs.
Energy company Drax Group said Tuesday it has signed an agreement with Brookfield and the asset manager's neocloud platform Radiant to jointly develop an AI data center on the Drax Power Station estate in North Yorkshire. London-listed shares of Drax were up 8.8% in early morning trading.
The project is initially targeting up to 100 megawatts of capacity to be operational from the first quarter of 2028, with an additional 500 MW of capacity to be brought online between 2028 and 2031. It is then looking to secure more than 1 gigawatt of capacity at the site by an unspecified date.
Brookfield estimates total investment, including semiconductors, could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion), with an initial £2.5 billion investment in phase 1.
"This is a unique opportunity for the UK's AI ecosystem to build at scale," Radiant CEO Mahdi Yahya said in a statement. "By designing, building and operating from the UK, it will give British researchers, startups and enterprises access to frontier compute at home."
The first phase of Brookfield's project in North Yorkshire will use power from the grid and target commercial customers from early 2028.
The initial phase is subject to planning, regulatory and network approvals from the government and relevant agencies, alongside securing a tenant for the project, Drax said in a statement said. The company added that final investment decisions are yet to be made.
While the U.S. has surged ahead on developing the huge data centers needed to power AI, Europe has been slower to break ground on the facilities. The U.K. in particular has struggled with high energy costs and challenges with long waiting times for businesses to connect to the grid.
In October, it was reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC at the time that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site."
Unlike the U.K., the Nordics benefit from abundant power and available land. Countries in the region, like Finland, have seen major commitments to develop AI data centers this year. In September, Google said it would invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) into AI infrastructure in the country, marking the tech giant's largest single investment in Europe.

items.summary: US Stock Market Fails To Recover as $700 Billion Comeback Collapses  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
US Stock Market Fails To Recover as $700 Billion Comeback Collapses
Wall Street appeared ready to recover from October's $2 trillion technology stock wipeout on Monday. Within hours, roughly $700 billion in fresh market gains had evaporated.
The S&P 500 surged as much as 1.1% in morning trading before closing down 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.1%, extending last week's brutal AI stock selloff.
The reversal came shortly after CNBC host Jim Cramer posted on X:
He was referring to Marvell's $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum. But the timing quickly revived jokes about Cramer's famously mixed market predictions.
Oil prices dropped to $104 as possible US-Iran peace talks raised hopes of cheaper energy and easing inflation.
Stocks initially jumped. The Nasdaq 100 gained around 1.3%, while the Dow climbed more than 1%.
But investors soon returned to the same concern that erased more than $2 trillion from the Nasdaq 100 during October: How much longer can Big Tech keep spending billions on AI without delivering sufficient returns?
Oracle plunged nearly 9% after announcing plans to raise $20 billion through stock and bond sales to fund its AI expansion. Marvell lost almost 13%.
Meanwhile, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett dismissed fears of an AI financing crisis.
"There's so much cash in the ecosystem that I think that people should be reassured," Hassett said.
Interestingly, nearly 70% of S&P 500 companies finished higher. The weakness remained concentrated in major technology stocks.
As for Cramer's supposed curse, the Inverse Cramer ETF, designed to bet against his recommendations, lost 15% before closing in 2024.
Investors now face Tuesday's US midterm elections and Friday's jobs report, with confidence in the AI trade already shaken.

items.title: Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision
items.summary: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel dies aged 30 after an on-field collision during a Spanish second-division match.
items.content:
Image caption, Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year deal
Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda," a club statement said.
"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, said: "With broken hearts and devastated, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his team-mates, friends, and to CD Tenerife."
Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."
De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way.
"We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."
Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss.
"My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."
Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe wrote on his social media: "Much sadness, there are no words."
Inter Miami and former Barcelona forward Lionel Messi said: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."
The Spanish football federation announced following De Miguel's death that Tuesday's Spanish Cup fixtures had been postponed.
Two fixtures in the first round of the men's Copa del Rey were due to be played, while Espanyol were set to take on AS Celtas in the women's Copa del Reina competition.
Image caption, De Miguel scored 11 goals in 29 matches for Tenerife
De Miguel, who was born in Madrid, started his career at Leganes in 2015 and went on to play for eight different clubs in Spain.
After spells with Lugo Fuenlabrada and Internacional Madrid, he returned to Fuenlabrada before stints at Union Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.
He joined Castellon in 2023 and scored 16 goals as the club achieved promotion to Spain's second division a year later.
The Spaniard joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the side.
De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernandez, who was born in 2025.

items.title: Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
items.summary: The two aircraft crashed just metres from the ground after trying to land at the same spot.
items.content:
Figure caption, Two helicopters collide in mid-air close to Mt Everest
An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
Image caption, People who witnessed the crash ran to the location of the helicopters afterwards
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

items.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
items.summary: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
items.content:
Figure caption, 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Image source, TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images
Image caption, Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
Image caption, An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butchers' shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

items.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
items.summary: The tech giant reports strong sales but admits "constraints" are affecting supplies of the iPhone Duo.
items.content:
Image caption, Chief executive John Ternus was presenting his first Apple results since taking over from Tim Cook
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.
The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.
The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".
Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.
Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.
It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen .
Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.
As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.
Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".
Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.
Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.
iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (Â£42bn).
Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.
Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.
The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.
Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.
Figure caption, Watch: Would you buy Apple's $2,000 foldable phone?
Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood".
Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%.
Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business.
While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive".
However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading.
